title: VB8-06917
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX 2018 appeal was reopened by the RAD following a determination that his claims should have been conducted with the assistance of a Designated Representative due to Mr.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I allow this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Mexico. Mr. XXXX alleges that he fears organized crime to whom he owes business debts. Since his arrival in Canada in 2017, Mr. XXXX has been diagnosed with XXXX.

Mr. XXXX was found not to be a refugee or a person in need of protection in his first claim in 2018. These decisions were based on section 97 and the viability of an internal flight alternative (IFA). Mr. XXXX XXXX 2018 appeal was reopened by the RAD following a determination that his claims should have been conducted with the assistance of a Designated Representative due to Mr. XXXX mental condition. I agree that the determinative issue is IFA.
The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.

Mr. XXXX XXXX alleges that he fears three groups: a cartel operating in his home region, an individual to whom he owes money and organized crime from his hometown. His initial claim for refugee protection was denied by the RPD as he was not found to have a nexus to the grounds set out in section 96 or 97 of the Act. He was also found to have a viable IFA in Mexico City. The RAD agreed to reopen his appeal due to a subsequent diagnosis of XXXX, which was found to have affected his ability to contest his appeal. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted

According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.2

The Appellant has provided several medical reports related to his diagnosis: Report of Dr. XXXX (XXXX XXXX 2019); Letter of XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX 2019), Attestation of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX 2019); Letter of Dr. XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX 2019); Letter from Dr. XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX 2020); and Letter of XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX 2020). These reports are admitted as, although they postdate the RPD decision, they could not reasonably have been provided prior to the decision. I also find that these reports are relevant to understanding the future medical needs of Mr. XXXX. They are new and credible reports from Canadian medical and professional sources.

The Appellant has also provided a number of objective reports about XXXX from the following Canadian sources : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ; XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX; XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX; XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ; XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. These reports are admitted as, although they postdate the RPD decision, they could not reasonably have been provided prior to the decision. These reports are relevant to understanding the future medical and social needs of Mr. XXXX. I find that they are credible based on their source, being known Canadian governmental or non-governmental organizations.

The Appellant has also provided a report from a Mexican source: "Abandoned and Disappeared: Mexico's Segregation and Abuse of Children and Adults with Disabilities" (2010). This report is admitted as, although it predates the RPD decision, it could not reasonably have been provided prior to the decision. This document is relevant to understanding the conditions for institutionalized medical care for mental health. It is credible from a known international organization, Disability Rights International.

The Appellant has also provided excerpts from the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Mexico. These documents already form part of the record of the objective evidence before the RAD. In addition, the specific excerpts quoted by the Appellant are consistent between August 30, 2019, and the 20th of September 2020 versions of the NDP. I find that I do not need to consider these documents as new evidence as they are already part of the record.
The Appellant is not seeking an oral hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3

The Appellant does not contest the RPD determination that Mr. XXXX did not meet the determination under section 97 of the Act. The Appellant argues that Mr. XXXX claim should be assessed under section 96 of the Act, as a Convention refugee, and that the determination of a viable IFA was incorrect based on his psychological condition.

An IFA is a determinative issue because, if a claimant can find safety from persecution by fleeing within Mexico, they are not entitled to Canada's surrogate protection.4 This is true for claims under section 96 or section 97. A claimant must be a refugee from a country, not from a particular region or city. Accordingly, the Appellant bears the onus to demonstrate that there is a serious possibility of persecution throughout the country, including the proposed IFA.5 The existence of a viable IFA is determinative of any refugee claim, whether under section 96 or 97.

The analysis for assessing an IFA has two parts.6 I must first determine whether there is a serious possibility that the Appellant will be persecuted, or whether he faces, on a balance of probabilities, a risk to his life, torture, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA. Secondly, I must also be satisfied, after considering the Appellant's individual circumstances and the conditions in the proposed IFA, that it would not be unreasonable to seek refuge in the IFA. An IFA will only be viable if both criterias are met.7 A high threshold of "nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area", applies equally to both parts of this test.8

The RPD proposed Mexico City as an IFA for Mr. XXXX. The law provides that once an IFA has been proposed, the Appellant bears the onus of proving that the IFA is not viable. For the following reasons, I find that the legal test for the Appellant fails on the second prong. a. It is safe for the Appellant in the proposed IFA.

The Appellant has a viable IFA where he does not face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk of harm in the proposed IFA. An IFA analysis requires a contextual approach, looking at the profile of the agents of harm, their motivation to search for the Appellant, and their ability to find him throughout Mexico. There can only be a serious possibility of persecution or a risk of harm if the agents of harm have both the "means and the motivation" to locate the Appellant.9

The Appellant has not provided new evidence that any of his agents of persecution are looking for him. I have reviewed the evidence provided at the RPD hearing as well as Mr. XXXX original narrative. None of the new evidence or the Appellant's submissions address this issue. Mr. XXXX has been in Canada since XXXX 2017. His evidence was that the most recent contact with any of the agents of persecution was in XXXX 2017. This length of time leads me to the conclusion that the agents of persecution are no longer interested in Mr. XXXX. I have also reviewed the alleged incident of computer tampering in 2018 and agree with the RPD's reasoning about this incident. I find that the incident of computer tampering in Calgary did not happen. On a balance of probabilities, I find that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that any of the agents of persecution have the means and motivation to find Mr. XXXX in the proposed IFA of Mexico City.

I am satisfied that the Appellant faces neither a serious possibility of persecution, nor, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture, a risk to his life, cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA. I now turn to the second part of the test to consider the reasonableness of the proposed IFA. b. It is reasonable for the Appellant to relocate to the proposed IFAs

The Federal Court in Adebayo explained that the high onus on the refugee claimant to demonstrate that a proposed IFA is unreasonable requires "nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area".10 I have reviewed the RPD's decision in light of the oral and written evidence from 2018 and the Appellant's memoranda. In my view, Mr. XXXX diagnosis, viewed in light of the objective conditions in Mexico, establishes that his life and safety would be jeopardized if he relocated to Mexico City.

The objective evidence sets out that Mexico has approximately 18 Million people with a disability in a population of 128 Million.11 Mexican law contains comprehensive garantees for people with disabilities.12 Disability rights have received significant public and political attention in recent years which have brought attention to the need to improve conditions for people with disabilities under state and national law.13 The Mexican government is taking steps to eradicate discrimination with mixed results. For example, Mexico was among the first countries to ratify the U.N. Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities,14 and has established the National Council for the Development and Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities (National Council) and other similar institutions at the state level.15

The evidence also shows that Mexico is having difficult implementing this legislation. Mental healthcare in Mexico is delivered predominantly through residential institutions. A report from Disability Rights International indicates that the primary reason for institutionalization is the lack of community-based services for people with disabilities.16 The evidence also shows that there are significant risks to the health and safety and human rights of people who are institutionalized.17 There is also evidence that the costs of medication are prohibitive, access to psychiatric care is limited and access to medications in the community is also limited.18

The Appellant is nearing middle age and has experienced precarious employment housing in Mexico and Canada19. Most importantly, he has significant ongoing mental health issues for which no cause has been determined and an ongoing course of medication is required.20 I have no evidence about the current or future support from his family which includes parents, siblings and an adult son, who do not live in Mexico City. His evidence was that he may have one first cousin who lived in Mexico City.21

The psychological evidence indicates that the Appellant meets the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia and continues to take medication for his illness and would not be able to function without this medication and treatment22. This assessment, and a letter from his social worker, opine that the Appellant's mental health would be exacerbated should he be re-exposed to the traumatic triggers and potential danger in Mexico.23 On a balance of probabilities, I find that these circumstances would make it difficult for the Appellant to find employment.

Further, the Appellant has no family support in Mexico City, the proposed IFA location. In the absence of any family support in the IFA and with his significant mental health issues, I find it more likely than not that the Appellant would face undue hardship in the area of accommodation.

I consider that the Appellant's psychological conditions will make it challenging for the Appellant to provide for himself. My assessment of the Appellants' circumstances is supported by the objective documentary evidence, which states that a disproportionate percentage of people with disabilities benefit from a social security system.24 I find it unlikely that the Appellant will have the means required to seek proper treatment for his severe mental health challenges without gainful employment. Given the severity of the Appellant's psychological impairment, I find that the unlikelihood that the Appellant will be able to access proper mental health treatment due to his circumstances meets the high threshold required to indicate that the IFA is not reasonable in the circumstances.
For these reasons, I do not find the proposed IFA location of Mexico City reasonable.

I grant the appeal and substitute my decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee and a person in need of protection.
